selected.spoken: Why water once climbed 524 metres up a mountain.

candidates.spoken: Why water once climbed 524 metres up a mountain.
The 1958 Lituya Bay earthquake occurred on July 9.
30 million cubic metres of rock caused it.
What If a Mountain Fell Into a Bay?
Lituya Bay is only 3 kilometres wide.
A local megatsunami strips slopes hundreds of metres up.
A massive rockslide plunged into a narrow bay.
It would not all happen at once.
An earthquake of magnitude 7.8 to 8.3 shook it loose.
Models put the wave crest itself at about 150 metres.
A large rockslide into a confined bay displaces water violently.
The water surged up the far slope.
So the tallest waves come from falling mountains.

script.spoken: Why water once climbed 524 metres up a mountain. 30 million cubic metres of rock caused it. An earthquake of magnitude 7.8 to 8.3 shook it loose. Lituya Bay is only 3 kilometres wide. The water surged up the far slope, stripping soil and trees. Models put the wave crest itself at about 150 metres. A narrow bay concentrates a landslide's push into one giant surge. So the tallest waves come from falling mountains, not earthquakes alone.
